LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

When royal weddings cost British taxpayers tens of millions of pounds, the press swoons over the "romance" and "tradition." When landed gentry throw extravagant debutante balls in heritage estates, it is framed as cultural heritage. But when two working-class kids from Liverpool earn their own fortune and choose to spend it celebrating their love in sunny Italy, the British establishment sneers. 

The implicit message from the critics was clear: *Know your place, and if you must get rich, at least have the decency to pretend you belong to our club.*

What makes the media’s vitriol particularly disgraceful is how conveniently critics ignored the astounding generosity at the heart of the occasion.

**The Class War in Ink: How British Tabloids Weaponized Wayne and Coleen Rooney’s Success**

In Britain, there is an unspoken rule regarding the social ladder: you are allowed to climb it, but you are not supposed to forget your place. Few public figures illustrate this cultural paradox more vividly than Wayne and Coleen Rooney. For over two decades, the boy from Croxteth who possessed a generational footballing talent and his childhood sweetheart have been staples of the British press. Yet, despite accumulating immense wealth, international fame, and a track record of quiet, extensive philanthropy, the couple has remained the ultimate target for a uniquely British form of media snobbery: classism.

To understand the tabloid obsession with the Rooneys is to understand Britain’s deep-seated anxiety about social mobility. In the meritocratic fantasy promised by modern sports and celebrity culture, working-class talent is celebrated. But when that talent translates into raw, unapologetic financial capital without the accompanying "refinement" of the traditional elite, the media establishment recoils. 

When Wayne Rooney exploded onto the global stage as a 16-year-old at Everton in 2002, he was undeniably a prodigy. Yet, almost instantly, the coverage of his athletic genius was shadowed by a persistent, patronizing narrative. Wayne was not just a brilliant footballer; he was framed as a "street fighter," a "bulldog," or an unpolished brute. His physical appearance and dialect were routinely mocked. Tabloids delighted in framing him as a "chav"—a pejorative term that reached its peak in the 2000s, designed specifically to demonize and ridicule the British working class.

Coleen, meanwhile, bore the brunt of a gendered, classist assault. Before she was praised for her sharp investigative instincts in the infamous "Wagatha Christie" saga, she was relentlessly hounded by paparazzi as the quintessential "WAG" (Wives and Girlfriends). Tabloid headlines tracked her shopping trips with predatory glee, framing her purchases not as the enviable lifestyle of a young, wealthy woman, but as tacky, vulgar spending by a girl who didn't know how to handle money. 

This double standard exposes the hypocrisy of tabloid coverage. When upper-class figures display lavish wealth, it is reported as grand tradition, heritage, or eccentric luxury. When a working-class couple from a Liverpool council estate buys a mansion, drives high-end cars, or wears designer clothes, it is branded as "gaudy" and "nouveau riche." The message from Fleet Street was clear: no matter how many Premier League titles Wayne won, or how many magazine covers Coleen graced, they were still just "common."

What makes this persistent mockery so egregious is how deliberately the media overlooked the couple’s substantial generosity. Long before athlete activism became mainstream, the Rooneys quietly used their fortune to support vulnerable communities. Through the Wayne Rooney Foundation, millions of pounds have been raised for charities including the NSPCC, Claire House Children’s Hospice, and Alder Hey Children’s Hospital in Liverpool. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Coleen and Wayne were among the first high-profile figures to make significant, unpublicized donations to local food banks and NHS trusts.

Yet, this philanthropy rarely fit the tabloids’ preferred narrative. A front-page story about Wayne’s generosity or Coleen’s hands-on charitable work did not sell papers in the way a sensationalized headline about a night out or a perceived fashion faux pas did. Generosity requires empathy, and empathy undermines the caricature the press worked so hard to build. By reducing the Rooneys to stereotypes of working-class indulgence, the media subtly reassured its readers that money could buy big houses, but it couldn't buy "class."

This coverage was never really about the Rooneys as individuals; it was about policing the boundaries of social status. The British tabloid press has long functioned as a cultural border guard, deciding who is "deserving" of their wealth and who remains a pretender. By continually reminding the public of Wayne and Coleen’s humble origins—using terms like "council house" or "common" as veiled insults—the press sought to keep them in their place.

Decades on, the narrative has begun to shift. Wayne is recognized as one of English football’s greatest-ever players, and Coleen has earned widespread public affection for her composure and authenticity. Yet, the history of their press coverage leaves a stain on British media culture. 

The story of Wayne and Coleen Rooney is ultimately a testament to resilience in the face of persistent snobbery. They achieved the British dream—rising from modest beginnings to the top of the world through sheer talent and determination—only to be mocked by an establishment that resented them for it. In attempting to belittle the Rooneys for being "common," the British tabloid media succeeded only in exposing the ugliness of its own elite anxiety.

**By [Author Name]**

Cast your mind back to June 2008. The venue was the 16th-century Villa Durazzo in Portofino, Italy. The sun was shining over the Italian Riviera, Marchesa silk was floating in the breeze, and thousands of butterflies were released into the Mediterranean sky.

It was the collective, collective wince of a middle-class media apparatus horrified by the sight of two working-class kids from Croxteth, Liverpool, spending their own hard-earned millions exactly how they wanted to.

In Britain, we claim to love a rags-to-riches story. We applaud the working-class hero who fights their way to the top through sheer, unadulterated talent. Wayne Rooney didn’t inherit a country estate; he kicked a battered football against street curbs until his boots wore out, turning himself into one of the most gifted footballers his generation ever produced. Coleen didn't rely on a trust fund; she navigated the brutal, feral UK tabloid ecosystem of the mid-2000s with remarkable poise, building a lucrative brand out of her own charisma and relatable charm.

You are supposed to pretend you’ve always belonged. 

Wayne and Coleen refused to play that game. They didn't want a quiet, apologetic ceremony in a drafty village church followed by lukewarm sherry. They wanted a jaw-dropping, lavish, unapologetic celebration of their love and their extraordinary rise. They wanted Portofino, yachts, Westlife performing, and yes, butterflies. 

And why on earth shouldn't they? 

The mockery of the butterfly theme was particularly telling. When an aristocrat spends hundreds of thousands of pounds on grand, archaic wedding traditions, the press calls it "hereditary majesty" or "timeless elegance." But when a young couple who grew up on a Liverpool council estate choose a dramatic, colorful motif, it’s branded "chavvy." 

Poetically, the butterfly was actually the perfect metaphor for the occasion. What is a butterfly if not a symbol of radical transformation? It was a celebration of two young people who had broken out of the socio-economic cocoon dictated by their birth, soaring to heights few ever achieve. The release of those butterflies wasn't tacky; it was a triumphant middle finger to the glass ceiling.

Wayne and Coleen used the media system that relentlessly stalked them to offset their costs and donate huge sums to charity, including £100,000 to Alder Hey Children’s Hospital in lieu of gifts. Fifteen years and four children later, their marriage has outlasted most of the cynical headlines written about them in 2008. Looking back, the butterflies weren't a sign of a lack of class—they were a symbol of freedom. And the critics? They were just mad they didn't get an invitation.
